questions.question: Your work on `feature` is done and you want it in `main`. Which sequence does that?
questions.explanation: `git merge X` brings X **into the current branch**. So switch to the branch that should receive the work first. Merging `main` into `feature` does the opposite: it brings `feature` up to date with `main`.

questions.question: When does `git merge feature` result in a **fast-forward** instead of a merge commit?
options: When the current branch has no new commits since `feature` branched off
When `feature` was pushed to the remote
questions.explanation: If the current branch is a direct ancestor of `feature`, Git just moves the branch label forward to `feature`'s tip. No merge commit is needed. If both branches have new commits, Git creates a merge commit with two parents.

questions.question: Your team wants every feature to show up as a merge commit in `main`, even when a fast-forward is possible. Which command?
questions.explanation: `--no-ff` always creates a merge commit, so the history shows which commits belonged to the feature, and the whole feature can be reverted in one go. `--ff-only` does the opposite: it refuses to merge unless a fast-forward is possible.

questions.question: You want to update local `main` to `origin/main`, but **only** if that doesn't create a merge commit. Which command?
questions.explanation: `--ff-only` fails instead of merging if your branch has diverged. Many people set `git config --global pull.ff only` so `git pull` never makes surprise merge commits.

questions.question: You ran `git merge feature` while on `main` and `price.py` has a conflict. Which line came from `main`?
options: Neither: the markers show the original version
questions.explanation: The part between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` is your current branch (`main`); the part between `=======` and `>>>>>>> feature` is the incoming branch. Edit the file to the version you want, and remove all three marker lines.

questions.question: You fixed the conflict in `price.py` and removed the markers. What's next to finish the merge?
questions.explanation: `git add` marks the conflict as resolved. Once every conflicted file is added, `git commit` (or `git merge --continue`) creates the merge commit with a prepared message. `git status` lists any files that are still `both modified`.

questions.question: A merge produced dozens of conflicts and you want to go back to how things were before you ran `git merge`. Which command?
questions.explanation: `git merge --abort` restores the state from before the merge. It works while the merge is still in progress (no merge commit yet). After the merge is committed, use `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` locally, or `git revert -m 1` if it's already pushed.

questions.question: During a merge of `feature` into `main`, `package-lock.json` conflicts. You simply want `feature`'s version of that whole file. Which command?
questions.explanation: During a merge, **ours** is the current branch (`main`) and **theirs** is the branch being merged (`feature`). `git restore --theirs <file>` works too. Careful: during a **rebase** the roles swap, because you're replaying your commits onto the other branch.

questions.question: `feature` has 23 messy commits. You want all its changes on `main` as **one** new commit. Which command, run on `main`?
questions.explanation: `--squash` stages the combined changes without committing and without recording a merge, so you commit them yourself as one commit. Because no merge is recorded, `git branch -d feature` will say it isn't merged; use `-D` once you've checked.

questions.question: How many parents does a normal merge commit have?
options: As many as the number of conflicts
questions.explanation: The first parent is the branch you were on, the second is the branch you merged. `git log --first-parent main` follows only the first parents, which gives a clean list of what landed on `main`. A regular commit has one parent, and the very first commit has none.

questions.question: Which three versions does Git compare in a three-way merge?
options: The tips of both branches and their common ancestor (the merge base)
The working tree, the index and `HEAD`
The local branch, the remote branch and the stash
The first, middle and last commit of the feature branch
questions.explanation: For each change, Git checks the merge base: if only one side changed a part, that change wins automatically. A conflict only happens when both sides changed the same lines differently. `git merge-base main feature` prints that ancestor.

questions.question: What does this do when `main` and `feature` changed the same lines?
options: Conflicting chunks are resolved with `feature`'s version; changes that don't conflict from both sides are kept
The whole result becomes exactly `feature`'s files, and `main`'s changes are dropped
The merge stops at the first conflict
questions.explanation: `-X ours` / `-X theirs` only decide **conflicting** chunks. Everything else merges normally. Don't confuse it with `-s ours`, a strategy that keeps your tree entirely and ignores the other branch's changes.

questions.question: In the middle of a large merge, which command prints just the names of the files that still have conflicts?
questions.explanation: `--diff-filter=U` keeps only unmerged files. `git status` shows them too, under "Unmerged paths" as `both modified`, but with everything else around them. `git mergetool` opens each conflicted file in a merge tool.

questions.question: You keep resolving the same conflict again and again, for example while repeatedly rebasing a long-lived branch. Which Git feature can remember your resolution and reuse it?
options: `rerere`, turned on with `git config --global rerere.enabled true`
questions.explanation: **rerere** stands for "reuse recorded resolution". Once enabled, Git records how you resolved each conflict and applies the same resolution automatically the next time it sees the identical conflict. Always check the result before committing.
